content.content:
---
name: impeccable
description: Use when the user wants to design, redesign, shape, critique, audit, polish, clarify, distill, harden, optimize, adapt, animate, colorize, extract, or otherwise improve a frontend interface. Covers websites, landing pages, dashboards, product UI, app shells, components, forms, settings, onboarding, and empty states. Handles UX review, visual hierarchy, information architecture, cognitive load, accessibility, performance, responsive behavior, theming, anti-patterns, typography, fonts, spacing, layout, alignment, color, motion, micro-interactions, UX copy, error states, edge cases, i18n, and reusable design systems or tokens. Also use for bland designs that need to become bolder or more delightful, loud designs that should become quieter, live browser iteration on UI elements, or ambitious visual effects that should feel technically extraordinary. Not for backend-only or non-UI tasks.
---

Designs and iterates production-grade frontend interfaces. Real working code, committed design choices, exceptional craft.

## Setup

You MUST do these steps before proceeding:

1. Run `node .agents/skills/impeccable/scripts/context.mjs` once per session. If you've already seen its output in this conversation, do not re-run it. The script either prints the project's PRODUCT.md (and DESIGN.md when present) as a markdown block, or tells you it's missing. Follow whatever it prints. **If it reports `NO_PRODUCT_MD`, stop and follow `reference/init.md` before doing anything else.** If the output ends with an `UPDATE_AVAILABLE` directive, follow it (ask the user once about updating, then continue). It never blocks the current task.
2. If the user invoked a sub-command (`craft`, `shape`, `audit`, `polish`, ...), you MUST read `reference/<command>.md` next. Non-optional. The reference defines the command's flow; without it you will skip steps the user expects.
3. Familiarize yourself with any existing design system, conventions, and components in the code. Read at least one project file (CSS / tokens / theme / a representative component or page). **Required even when you've loaded a sub-command reference in step 2.** Don't reinvent the wheel; use what's there when it works, branch out when the UX wins.
4. Read the matching register reference. **This is non-optional; skipping it produces generic output.** If the project is marketing, a landing page, a campaign, long-form content, or a portfolio (design IS the product), read `reference/brand.md`. If it is app UI, admin, a dashboard, or a tool (design SERVES the product), read `reference/product.md`. Pick by first match: (1) task cue ("landing page" vs "dashboard"); (2) surface in focus (the page, file, or route being worked on); (3) `register` field in PRODUCT.md.
5. **If the project is brand-new (no existing CSS tokens / theme / committed brand colors found in step 3)**, run `node .agents/skills/impeccable/scripts/palette.mjs` to receive a brand seed color and composition guidance. This is the anchor for your primary brand color. Compose the rest of the palette (bg, surface, ink, accent, muted) around it per the script's instructions. Use OKLCH throughout. **Skip this step only if step 3 found committed brand colors in existing tokens; in that case identity-preservation wins.**

## Design guidance

Produce ready-to-ship, production-grade code, not prototypes or starting points. Take no shortcuts unless the user asks for them (when in doubt, ask). Don't stop until arriving at a complete implementation (beautiful, responsive, fast, precise, bug-free, on brand). You take attention to detail seriously: every page, section or component crafted is battle tested using the tools available to you (browser screenshotting, computer use, etc). GPT is capable of extraordinary work. Don't hold back.

### General rules

#### Color

- **Verify contrast.** Body text must hit ≥4.5:1 against its background; large text (≥18px or bold ≥14px) needs ≥3:1. Placeholder text needs the same 4.5:1, not the muted-gray default. The most common failure: muted gray body text on a tinted near-white. If the contrast is even close, bump the body color toward the ink end of the ramp; light gray "for elegance" is the single biggest reason AI designs feel hard to read.
- Gray text on a colored background looks washed out. Use a darker shade of the background's own hue, or a transparency of the text color.

#### Typography

- Cap body line length at 65–75ch.
- Hierarchy through scale + weight contrast (≥1.25 ratio between steps). Avoid flat scales.
- Cap font-family count at 3 (display + body + optional mono). More than 3 reads as indecision, not richness. One well-tuned family with weight contrast usually beats three competing typefaces.
- Don't pair fonts that are similar but not identical (two geometric sans-serifs, two humanist sans-serifs). Pair on a contrast axis (serif + sans, geometric + humanist) or use one family in multiple weights.
- No all-caps body copy. Reserve uppercase for short labels (≤4 words), section eyebrows (used sparingly per the Absolute bans), and badges. Sentences in ALL CAPS are unreadable at body sizes.
- Hero / display heading ceiling: clamp() max ≤ 6rem (~96px). Above that the page is shouting, not designing.
- Display heading letter-spacing floor: ≥ -0.04em. Anything tighter and letters touch; cramped, not "designed".

Two hard typographic ceilings you currently miss:
- Hero clamp() max ≤ 6rem. 8–11rem (128–176px) reads as comically loud, not bold.
- Display letter-spacing ≥ -0.04em. Your default of -0.05 to -0.085em on display H1s makes the letters touch and reads as cramped. -0.02 to -0.03em is plenty for tight grotesque display; -0.04em is the floor.

#### Layout

- Vary spacing for rhythm.
- Cards are the lazy answer. Use them only when they're truly the best affordance. Nested cards are always wrong.
- Flexbox for 1D, Grid for 2D. Don't default to Grid when `flex-wrap` would be simpler.
- For responsive grids without breakpoints: `repeat(auto-fit, minmax(280px, 1fr))`.
- Build a semantic z-index scale (dropdown → sticky → modal-backdrop → modal → toast → tooltip). Never arbitrary values like 999 or 9999.

#### Motion
- Motion should be intentional, and not be an afterthought. consider it as part of the build.
- Don't animate CSS layout properties unless truly needed.
- Ease out with exponential curves (ease-out-quart / quint / expo). No bounce, no elastic.
- Use libraries for more advanced motion needs (e.g. motion, gsap, anime.js, lenis etc)
- Reduced motion is not optional. Every animation needs a `@media (prefers-reduced-motion: reduce)` alternative: typically a crossfade or instant transition.
- Staggering the items within one list is legitimate. The tell is the uniform reflex (one identical entrance applied to every section), not motion itself; each reveal should fit what it reveals. Suppressing the reflex is never a reason to ship a page with no motion at all.
- Reveal animations must enhance an already-visible default. Don't gate content visibility on a class-triggered transition; transitions pause on hidden tabs and headless renderers, so the reveal never fires and the section ships blank.
- Premium motion materials are not just transform/opacity. Blur, backdrop-filter, clip-path, mask, and shadow/glow are part of the palette when they materially improve the effect and stay smooth.

#### Interaction

- Dropdowns rendered with `position: absolute` inside an `overflow: hidden` or `overflow: auto` container will be clipped. Use the native `<dialog>` / popover API, `position: fixed`, or a portal to escape the stacking context.

### Copy

- Every word earns its place. No restated headings, no intros that repeat the title.
- **No em dashes.** Use commas, colons, semicolons, periods, or parentheses. Also not `--`.
- **No aphoristic-cadence body copy as a default voice.** Don't fall into the rhythm of "serious statement, then punchy short negation" as the page's recurring voice. If three or more section copy blocks on the page land on a short rebuttal-shaped sentence, rewrite. Specific, not aphoristic.
- **No marketing buzzwords.** The streamline / empower / supercharge / leverage / unleash / transform / seamless / world-class / enterprise-grade / next-generation / cutting-edge / game-changer / mission-critical family of phrases. Pick a specific noun and a verb that describes what the product literally does.
- Button labels: verb + object. "Save changes" beats "OK"; "Delete project" beats "Yes". The label should say what will happen.
- Link text needs standalone meaning. "View pricing plans" beats "Click here"; screen readers announce links out of context.

### New projects only (when no prior work exists)

#### Color & Theme

- Use OKLCH.
- **The cream / sand / beige body bg is the saturated AI default of 2026.** The whole warm-neutral band (OKLCH L 0.84-0.97, C < 0.06, hue 40-100) reads as cream/sand/paper/parchment regardless of what you call it. Token names like `--paper`, `--cream`, `--sand`, `--bone`, `--flour`, `--linen`, `--parchment`, `--wheat`, `--biscuit`, `--ivory` are tells in themselves. If the brief is "warm, traditional, family-coastal-Italian" or "magazine-warm" or "editorial-restraint", DO NOT translate that into a near-white warm-tinted bg; that's the AI move. Pick: (a) a saturated brand color as the body (terracotta, oxblood, deep ochre, near-black), (b) a true off-white at chroma 0 (or chroma toward the brand's own hue, not toward warmth-by-default), or (c) a darker mid-tone tinted neutral that's clearly the brand's own. "Warmth" in the brand is carried by accent + typography + imagery, not by body bg.
- Tinted neutrals: add 0.005–0.015 chroma toward the brand's hue. Don't default-tint toward warm or cool "because the brand feels that way"; that's the cross-project monoculture move.
- When picking a theme: Dark vs. light is never a default. Not dark "because tools look cool dark." Not light "to be safe.".Before choosing, write one sentence of physical scene: who uses this, where, under what ambient light, in what mood. If the sentence doesn't force the answer, it's not concrete enough. Add detail until it does.
- Pick a **color strategy** before picking colors. Four steps on the commitment axis:
  - **Restrained**: tinted neutrals + one accent ≤10%. Product default; brand minimalism.
  - **Committed**: one saturated color carries 30–60% of the surface. Brand default for identity-driven pages.
  - **Full palette**: 3–4 named roles, each used deliberately. Brand campaigns; product data viz.
  - **Drenched**: the surface IS the color. Brand heroes, campaign pages.

### Absolute bans

Match-and-refuse. If you're about to write any of these, rewrite the element with different structure.

- **Side-stripe borders.** `border-left` or `border-right` greater than 1px as a colored accent on cards, list items, callouts, or alerts. Never intentional. Rewrite with full borders, background tints, leading numbers/icons, or nothing.
- **Gradient text.** `background-clip: text` combined with a gradient background. Decorative, never meaningful. Use a single solid color. Emphasis via weight or size.
- **Glassmorphism as default.** Blurs and glass cards used decoratively. Rare and purposeful, or nothing.
- **The hero-metric template.** Big number, small label, supporting stats, gradient accent. SaaS cliché.
- **Identical card grids.** Same-sized cards with icon + heading + text, repeated endlessly.
- **Tiny uppercase tracked eyebrow above every section.** The 2023-era kicker (small all-caps text with wide tracking, "ABOUT" "PROCESS" "PRICING" above each heading) is now the saturated AI scaffold; it appears on 55-95% of generations regardless of brief, which is the definition of a tell. One named kicker as a deliberate brand system is voice; an eyebrow on every section is AI grammar. Choose a different cadence.
- **Numbered section markers as default scaffolding (01 / 02 / 03).** Putting `01 · About / 02 · Process / 03 · Pricing` above every section is the eyebrow trope one tier deeper: reach for it because "landing pages do this" and you're scaffolding by reflex. Numbers earn their place when the section actually IS a sequence (a real 3-step process, an ordered flow, a typed timeline) and the order carries information the reader needs. One deliberate numbered sequence on one page is voice; numbered eyebrows on every section across the site is AI grammar.
- **Text that overflows its container.** Long heading words plus large clamp scales plus narrow grids cause headline overflow on tablet/mobile. Test the heading copy at every breakpoint; if it overflows, reduce the clamp max or rewrite the copy. The viewport is part of the design.

**Codex-specific defects** (your most-frequent giveaways; refuse-and-rewrite):

- **`border: 1px solid X` + `box-shadow: 0 Npx Mpx ...` with M ≥ 16px** on the same element. The "ghost-card" pattern: 1px border plus soft wide drop shadow on buttons and cards. Don't pair them. Pick one (a single solid border at the brand color, OR a defined shadow at no more than 8px blur), never both as decoration.
- **`border-radius: 32px+` on cards / sections / inputs.** You over-round. Cards top out at 12–16px; full-pill is fine for tags/buttons. Picking 24/28/32/40px on a card is the codex tell; no brand wants "insanely rounded".
- **Hand-drawn / sketchy SVG illustrations.** Class names like `loose-sketch`, `*-sketch`, `doodle`, `wavy`; `feTurbulence` / `feDisplacementMap` "paper grain" filters; 5-to-30 path crude scenes meant to depict a tangible subject (an otter, a table-and-fork, an album cover). All of these read as amateurish, not whimsical. If you can't render the scene with real assets, ship no illustration. Don't attempt sketchy SVG as a fallback.
- **`repeating-linear-gradient(...)` stripe backgrounds.** Diagonal stripes in `body:before` or section backgrounds are pure codex decoration. Don't.
- **"X theater" / "actually X" / "not just X, it's Y" copy.** "Productivity theater", "engagement theater", "growth theater": instant AI slop. Choose a specific noun, not a meta-criticism phrase.

### The AI slop test

If someone could look at this interface and say "AI made that" without doubt, it's failed. Cross-register failures are the absolute bans above. Register-specific failures live in each reference.

**Category-reflex check.** Run at two altitudes; the second one catches what the first one misses.

- **First-order:** if someone could guess the theme + palette from the category alone, it's the first training-data reflex. Rework the scene sentence and color strategy until the answer isn't obvious from the domain.
- **Second-order:** if someone could guess the aesthetic family from category-plus-anti-references ("AI workflow tool that's not SaaS-cream → editorial-typographic", "fintech that's not navy-and-gold → terminal-native dark mode"), it's the trap one tier deeper. The first reflex was avoided; the second wasn't. Rework until both answers are not obvious. The brand register's [reflex-reject aesthetic lanes](reference/brand.md) list catches the currently-saturated families.

## Commands

| Command | Category | Description | Reference |
|---|---|---|---|
| `craft [feature]` | Build | Shape, then build a feature end-to-end | [reference/craft.md](reference/craft.md) |
| `shape [feature]` | Build | Plan UX/UI before writing code | [reference/shape.md](reference/shape.md) |
| `init` | Build | Set up project context: PRODUCT.md, DESIGN.md, live config, next steps | [reference/init.md](reference/init.md) |
| `document` | Build | Generate DESIGN.md from existing project code | [reference/document.md](reference/document.md) |
| `extract [target]` | Build | Pull reusable tokens and components into design system | [reference/extract.md](reference/extract.md) |
| `critique [target]` | Evaluate | UX design review with heuristic scoring | [reference/critique.md](reference/critique.md) |
| `audit [target]` | Evaluate | Technical quality checks (a11y, perf, responsive) | [reference/audit.md](reference/audit.md) |
| `polish [target]` | Refine | Final quality pass before shipping | [reference/polish.md](reference/polish.md) |
| `bolder [target]` | Refine | Amplify safe or bland designs | [reference/bolder.md](reference/bolder.md) |
| `quieter [target]` | Refine | Tone down aggressive or overstimulating designs | [reference/quieter.md](reference/quieter.md) |
| `distill [target]` | Refine | Strip to essence, remove complexity | [reference/distill.md](reference/distill.md) |
| `harden [target]` | Refine | Production-ready: errors, i18n, edge cases | [reference/harden.md](reference/harden.md) |
| `onboard [target]` | Refine | Design first-run flows, empty states, activation | [reference/onboard.md](reference/onboard.md) |

## Design guidance

Produce ready-to-ship, production-grade code, not prototypes or starting points. Take no shortcuts unless the user asks for them (when in doubt, ask). Don't stop until arriving at a complete implementation (beautiful, responsive, fast, precise, bug-free, on brand). You take attention to detail seriously: every page, section or component crafted is battle tested using the tools available to you (browser screenshotting, computer use, etc). GPT is capable of extraordinary work. Don't hold back.

### General rules

#### Color

- **Verify contrast.** Body text must hit ≥4.5:1 against its background; large text (≥18px or bold ≥14px) needs ≥3:1. Placeholder text needs the same 4.5:1, not the muted-gray default. The most common failure: muted gray body text on a tinted near-white. If the contrast is even close, bump the body color toward the ink end of the ramp; light gray "for elegance" is the single biggest reason AI designs feel hard to read.
- Gray text on a colored background looks washed out. Use a darker shade of the background's own hue, or a transparency of the text color.

#### Typography

- Cap body line length at 65–75ch.
- Hierarchy through scale + weight contrast (≥1.25 ratio between steps). Avoid flat scales.
- Cap font-family count at 3 (display + body + optional mono). More than 3 reads as indecision, not richness. One well-tuned family with weight contrast usually beats three competing typefaces.
- Don't pair fonts that are similar but not identical (two geometric sans-serifs, two humanist sans-serifs). Pair on a contrast axis (serif + sans, geometric + humanist) or use one family in multiple weights.
- No all-caps body copy. Reserve uppercase for short labels (≤4 words), section eyebrows (used sparingly per the Absolute bans), and badges. Sentences in ALL CAPS are unreadable at body sizes.
- Hero / display heading ceiling: clamp() max ≤ 6rem (~96px). Above that the page is shouting, not designing.
- Display heading letter-spacing floor: ≥ -0.04em. Anything tighter and letters touch; cramped, not "designed".

Two hard typographic ceilings you currently miss:
- Hero clamp() max ≤ 6rem. 8–11rem (128–176px) reads as comically loud, not bold.
- Display letter-spacing ≥ -0.04em. Your default of -0.05 to -0.085em on display H1s makes the letters touch and reads as cramped. -0.02 to -0.03em is plenty for tight grotesque display; -0.04em is the floor.

#### Layout

- Vary spacing for rhythm.
- Cards are the lazy answer. Use them only when they're truly the best affordance. Nested cards are always wrong.
- Flexbox for 1D, Grid for 2D. Don't default to Grid when `flex-wrap` would be simpler.
- For responsive grids without breakpoints: `repeat(auto-fit, minmax(280px, 1fr))`.
- Build a semantic z-index scale (dropdown → sticky → modal-backdrop → modal → toast → tooltip). Never arbitrary values like 999 or 9999.

#### Motion
- Motion should be intentional, and not be an afterthought. consider it as part of the build.
- Don't animate CSS layout properties unless truly needed.
- Ease out with exponential curves (ease-out-quart / quint / expo). No bounce, no elastic.
- Use libraries for more advanced motion needs (e.g. motion, gsap, anime.js, lenis etc)
- Reduced motion is not optional. Every animation needs a `@media (prefers-reduced-motion: reduce)` alternative: typically a crossfade or instant transition.
- Staggering the items within one list is legitimate. The tell is the uniform reflex (one identical entrance applied to every section), not motion itself; each reveal should fit what it reveals. Suppressing the reflex is never a reason to ship a page with no motion at all.
- Reveal animations must enhance an already-visible default. Don't gate content visibility on a class-triggered transition; transitions pause on hidden tabs and headless renderers, so the reveal never fires and the section ships blank.
- Premium motion materials are not just transform/opacity. Blur, backdrop-filter, clip-path, mask, and shadow/glow are part of the palette when they materially improve the effect and stay smooth.

#### Interaction

- Dropdowns rendered with `position: absolute` inside an `overflow: hidden` or `overflow: auto` container will be clipped. Use the native `<dialog>` / popover API, `position: fixed`, or a portal to escape the stacking context.

### Copy

- Every word earns its place. No restated headings, no intros that repeat the title.
- **No em dashes.** Use commas, colons, semicolons, periods, or parentheses. Also not `--`.
- **No aphoristic-cadence body copy as a default voice.** Don't fall into the rhythm of "serious statement, then punchy short negation" as the page's recurring voice. If three or more section copy blocks on the page land on a short rebuttal-shaped sentence, rewrite. Specific, not aphoristic.
- **No marketing buzzwords.** The streamline / empower / supercharge / leverage / unleash / transform / seamless / world-class / enterprise-grade / next-generation / cutting-edge / game-changer / mission-critical family of phrases. Pick a specific noun and a verb that describes what the product literally does.
- Button labels: verb + object. "Save changes" beats "OK"; "Delete project" beats "Yes". The label should say what will happen.
- Link text needs standalone meaning. "View pricing plans" beats "Click here"; screen readers announce links out of context.

### New projects only (when no prior work exists)

#### Color & Theme

- Use OKLCH.
- **The cream / sand / beige body bg is the saturated AI default of 2026.** The whole warm-neutral band (OKLCH L 0.84-0.97, C < 0.06, hue 40-100) reads as cream/sand/paper/parchment regardless of what you call it. Token names like `--paper`, `--cream`, `--sand`, `--bone`, `--flour`, `--linen`, `--parchment`, `--wheat`, `--biscuit`, `--ivory` are tells in themselves. If the brief is "warm, traditional, family-coastal-Italian" or "magazine-warm" or "editorial-restraint", DO NOT translate that into a near-white warm-tinted bg; that's the AI move. Pick: (a) a saturated brand color as the body (terracotta, oxblood, deep ochre, near-black), (b) a true off-white at chroma 0 (or chroma toward the brand's own hue, not toward warmth-by-default), or (c) a darker mid-tone tinted neutral that's clearly the brand's own. "Warmth" in the brand is carried by accent + typography + imagery, not by body bg.
- Tinted neutrals: add 0.005–0.015 chroma toward the brand's hue. Don't default-tint toward warm or cool "because the brand feels that way"; that's the cross-project monoculture move.
- When picking a theme: Dark vs. light is never a default. Not dark "because tools look cool dark." Not light "to be safe.".Before choosing, write one sentence of physical scene: who uses this, where, under what ambient light, in what mood. If the sentence doesn't force the answer, it's not concrete enough. Add detail until it does.
- Pick a **color strategy** before picking colors. Four steps on the commitment axis:
  - **Restrained**: tinted neutrals + one accent ≤10%. Product default; brand minimalism.
  - **Committed**: one saturated color carries 30–60% of the surface. Brand default for identity-driven pages.
  - **Full palette**: 3–4 named roles, each used deliberately. Brand campaigns; product data viz.
  - **Drenched**: the surface IS the color. Brand heroes, campaign pages.

### Absolute bans

Match-and-refuse. If you're about to write any of these, rewrite the element with different structure.

- **Side-stripe borders.** `border-left` or `border-right` greater than 1px as a colored accent on cards, list items, callouts, or alerts. Never intentional. Rewrite with full borders, background tints, leading numbers/icons, or nothing.
- **Gradient text.** `background-clip: text` combined with a gradient background. Decorative, never meaningful. Use a single solid color. Emphasis via weight or size.
- **Glassmorphism as default.** Blurs and glass cards used decoratively. Rare and purposeful, or nothing.
- **The hero-metric template.** Big number, small label, supporting stats, gradient accent. SaaS cliché.
- **Identical card grids.** Same-sized cards with icon + heading + text, repeated endlessly.
- **Tiny uppercase tracked eyebrow above every section.** The 2023-era kicker (small all-caps text with wide tracking, "ABOUT" "PROCESS" "PRICING" above each heading) is now the saturated AI scaffold; it appears on 55-95% of generations regardless of brief, which is the definition of a tell. And with four tabs, compare, context, and ask-room features, there's a lot of UI overhead for editing a single sentence—when the writer could just edit directly in the manuscript with undo, since the textarea's only real advantages over the editor are surfacing earlier wordings and text-to-speech playback.

The honest labeling that meaning hasn't been checked is admirable but means every option comes with a caveat—the bench offers choices without judgment, acting as a picker rather than a critic. It's also scoped to the sentence level, when a writer's real stuckness is usually about the sentence's job in the paragraph—its transition, claim, or image—not its surface wording. I'm thinking about what research says writers actually do when stuck: Sommers' and Flower & Hayes' work shows experienced writers revise for meaning and structure while students fixate on word choice, and Elbow's advice to read aloud and identify the sentence's function points toward a different kind of tool entirely.

I want to verify these as real citable sources via search, and maybe reference Grammarly's rewrite feature as an example of the generic picker to contrast against, plus something like Scrivener's snapshots for versioning precedent—keeping external claims to just two or three, verified ones. My recommendation is forming around having the bench open with a single question—"what should this sentence do here?"—letting the writer name the job (or pick from a few offered options like setting up a claim or answering a prior question), then generating candidates based on that stated intent rather than just surface rewordings.

Actually I think there's a stronger version: instead of a wording picker, the bench becomes a "sentence job" check from the reader's side—showing a one-line paraphrase of what the sentence actually conveys and what the next sentence needs from it, so the writer can compare intention against effect and then choose to keep, rewrite with the gap named, cut, or move it. This fits Sommers' point that experienced writers revise with the reader's understanding in mind, and matches the brief's push for every card to support a real decision.

What a writer really needs when rewriting an opening line nine times isn't more alternatives but a diagnosis of what's actually wrong—like a sentence trying to do two jobs at once (setting the scene vs. establishing grief) and not knowing which to lead with. A good editor would point out the pattern across drafts: "your attempts keep alternating between grief-first and setting-first," turning the existing attempt ledger into real diagnostic evidence that nothing else in the tool provides, since Jev can classify these drafts cheaply.

Even without a text-generation model, I could compute a pure data comparison across all the draft wordings — finding what stays constant versus what keeps shifting between attempts. That "churn map" alone could tell a writer something true and useful: "your opening clause has stayed the same across five tries, but you keep rewriting the ending," which is a genuine diagnosis drawn purely from the attempt history.

For the interaction design, I'm thinking the trigger could be a quiet margin note tied to the same struggle signal — something like "you've reworded this 4 times; the ending keeps changing" — which opens on click or via a "Rework" selection. The visible output would show the stable portion of the sentence in plain text with the contested span highlighted, alongside short fragment-level variants of just that contested piece rather than full rewritten sentences.

Each variant gets one action — preview in place or use — plus a line stating what the next sentence needs from this one. The writer's decision is to pick an ending, keep the current one, or cut/move on, which settles the ledger entry so the bench stops firing (a kind of feedback memory). Applying should support undo, return focus to the sentence's end, and clear the tick with a cooldown.

I also want to cut some existing surface area: fold the Words tab into the selection menu since alternatives already live there, either drop or shrink the Place tab since the 3-moves trigger could become its own tiny instrument, and remove the side-by-side compare view since diff already covers that.

I'm second-guessing how aggressively to cut — "Hear" is cheap and the design doc values it, so I'll leave it as a single button rather than a tab. I should confirm the editor already supports an in-place preview ghost — checking previewVariant, and yes, it draws one. I also want to sanity-check hit rate on real prose; I could run the candidate-generation logic against a sample paragraph via a quick script, which would be read-only and safe, though I need to watch for import issues with inline CSS in the bench module.

I'm weighing whether to pull in outside research — maybe worth checking Sommers (1980) and Flower & Hayes' 1986 work on revision strategies as citations, while skipping any comparison to Grammarly's rewrite picker since the user already ruled that out explicitly.

The detection-versus-diagnosis distinction really is the crux here: my current approach supports detecting that something's stuck and offering alternatives, but it skips the diagnosis step entirely. I want to verify this by checking several things — the flow-surface code, PRODUCT.md, the selection-actions rework label, spoken-text references, the instrument-evaluation doc, word variants, the generation provider, and running a quick tsx experiment, plus a couple of web searches.

# Product

## Register

product

## Users

Writers, editors, researchers, and technically comfortable creators who want a focused drafting room with structured editorial feedback. They are usually trying to move from a vague brief or partial draft into a clearer manuscript, then export or publish it.

## Product Purpose

Twyne is a local-first writing desk with an AI-assisted room of editors. It helps writers define a project dossier, draft in rich text, receive persona feedback, score work against a rubric, manage citations, sync across devices when signed in, and publish or export finished work. Success means the writer keeps ownership and momentum while the product makes revision concrete.

## Brand Personality

Editorial, exacting, literary. The product should feel like a working writer's room rather than generic SaaS: opinionated, calm, and serious about craft without getting precious.

## Anti-references

Do not make Twyne look like a generic AI chat app, a growth dashboard, a blank note-taking clone, or a loud marketing funnel. Avoid decorative UI that competes with the manuscript, vague AI productivity claims, and controls that obscure where drafts and keys are stored.

## Design Principles

- Keep the manuscript central.
- Make data movement explicit: local, synced, published, or sent to a provider.
- Use standard controls for standard tasks, dressed in Twyne's editorial system.
- Prefer concise copy that names the actual action.
- Preserve writer trust through clear export, privacy, and account controls.

## Accessibility & Inclusion

Aim for WCAG AA contrast and keyboard-operable controls. Important interactions should work with semantic HTML where possible. Respect reduced-motion preferences, avoid color-only state, and keep long-form reading comfortable on mobile and desktop.

# Writing instruments: evaluation and review

The checks are deliberately separate. A rule passing does not establish model quality;
a model returning text does not establish a good edit; a scheduled job test does not
establish a live provider task surviving a closed browser tab.

## Reproduce the local corpus and benchmark

```sh
rtk proxy bun run eval:instruments
rtk proxy bun run eval:instruments --case scene --no-benchmark
rtk proxy bun run bench:instruments --strict-performance --max-p95-ms 250
```

`evals/instruments/corpus.ts` contains authored, fictional fixtures with expected
findings and protected names, numbers and negation. The runner checks complete
rewrites, exact source offsets, settled history, duplicates versus semantic claims,
scene evidence versus proposed details, bounded paragraph/entity requests, explicit
instruction constraints, pinned local model manifests, and cancellation/source
contracts with fake transports. No account or model call occurs in this suite.

JSON and Markdown reports under `artifacts/instrument-evals/` contain the revision,
dirty state, corpus hash, runtime/CPU, per-case failures, all timing samples and flags.
`--output <directory>` chooses a stable result directory. An unknown `--case` fails.
The benchmark measures segmentation, analysis and score calculation at 500, 5,000
and 10,000 words. It separates first pass from six warmups and 50 samples, reporting
p50/p95/p99. These are analysis times, **not typing latency**. The default 250ms p95
flag is a broad regression threshold; use the same machine for useful comparisons.

## Which editor should weigh in?

```sh
rtk proxy bun run eval:room-routing
rtk proxy bun run eval:room-routing --case sentence-smallest-cut
```

`evals/instruments/room-routing-corpus.ts` contains ten authored, fictional Sentence,
Threads and Scene questions. Each names an acceptable set of editor IDs, including
one question where `none` is required. These are inspectable reference judgments,
not an objective measure of good writing. The default command validates the corpus
and builds the exact application requests with **zero network calls**, even when
an endpoint is configured. It reports model quality as `not-run`.

To measure actual model routing, explicitly opt in and supply a System One endpoint:

```sh
rtk proxy bun run eval:room-routing --run-model --endpoint https://your-endpoint.example --model jev-latest
```

The runner also accepts `TWYNE_ROOM_ROUTING_ENDPOINT` and `TWYNE_ROOM_ROUTING_MODEL`;
credentials are accepted only through `TWYNE_ROOM_ROUTING_API_KEY`, never a command
argument. Live execution sends only the authored fictional cases and can incur
provider charges. JSON and Markdown retain revision, dirty state, corpus and request
hashes, selected IDs, full distributions, confidence, request timing and failures.
Malformed distributions and choices outside the authored acceptable sets are flagged.
An unknown case or live run without an endpoint fails before any request. This
evaluates editor selection; it does not score the resulting editor's prose.

Search results confirm the citation details and summarize the article:

**Bibliographic details:** Sommers, Nancy. College Composition and Communication, v31 n4 p378-88 Dec 1980 (ERIC EJ240356). Published by: National Council of Teachers of English, Stable URL: http://www.jstor.org/stable/356588; DOI:10.2307/356588.

**ERIC abstract:** The article explores the flaws in linear theories of the writing process and student writers' attitudes toward revision that these theories reinforce. It discusses the revision strategies of experienced writers, showing that the writing process is recursive rather than linear.

**Opening lines of the article:** Although various aspects of the writing process have been studied extensively of late, research on revision has been notably absent. The reason for this, I suspect, is that current models of the writing process have directed attention away from revision.

**Study design (from secondary summaries):** Sommers shares the results of a study she had conducted with twenty university freshmen (referred to as "student writers") and twenty experienced adult writers (referred to as "experienced writers"). The study included twenty freshmen from Boston University and the University of Oklahoma with SAT verbal scores from 450-600, and twenty experienced writers, including editors and journalists. Four revision operations were identified: deletion, substitution, addition, and reordering. Also four levels of changes were identified: word, phrase, sentence, and theme.

**Key finding:** The students, Sommers discovered, understood the revision process as merely a "rewording activity." On the other hand, experienced writers described their revision process as cyclical steps, involving many revision drafts where their focus is to find the main idea and elaborate after a series of addition and deletion of ideas.

A full-text PDF is available at spalding.pbworks.com (http://spalding.pbworks.com/f/Sommers_Revision+Strategies.pdf), and the ERIC record is at https://eric.ed.gov/?id=EJ240356. Note that one secondary source cites the page range as 378–387, but ERIC, JSTOR, and most citations give 378–388.

I have what I need to write the report now. Since this goes to the parent orchestrator as the deliverable, I'll keep it substantial but readable, limiting myself to a few headers with bold lead-ins for subsections, avoiding em-dashes, and using a table for the probe data.

I want to get the mechanics precise: the trigger fires when a writer has three or more settled rewrites of a passage (tracked via the ledger of complete, spell-checked wordings with enough distance between them), passing a struggle threshold and classification gate, with related triggers for repeated placements or selection-based rework/alternatives. On the content side, the rewrite tab pulls the writer's earlier settled wordings plus a set of regex-based rules, emphasis and semicolon splitting, and time-clause fronting, capped at a handful of suggested modes.

Beyond that, the bench surfaces provider-generated variants (reorder/cut/make-concrete prompts), Harper-gated and optionally scored by Jev for meaning probability, shown only inside a "how these were checked" disclosure, alongside preview ghosts, a compare panel, and a diff-based working textarea with undo and a cooldown. There's also a words panel with bundled headwords and dotted repeats, a "place" feature for repositioning, a "hear" TTS mode, and an "ask an editor" path routed through Jev personas. I'm double-checking whether a "say it" spoken-candidate UI actually exists in the bench — I found the controller method but no matching UI reference in the files I grepped, so I want to avoid overclaiming that feature exists.

Looking at my probe test — only 8 sentences, with rules firing mainly on the ones I deliberately planted — I realize this is illustrative rather than a real measurement. Using the Flower et al. detection/diagnosis framework, I'm noting that the bench handles detection and offers solution alternatives but never actually diagnoses what's wrong with the sentence or what it needs to accomplish.

Drawing on Sommers' distinction between experienced writers (who revise for meaning and reader) versus students (who treat revision as rewording), I think the bench is built entirely for that rewording model — someone who's already rejected several wordings gets nothing new from seeing surface transforms again. I'm marking this as an inference, not actual user research: the "can't see myself using it" reaction likely stems from this gap. There's also too much surface complexity relative to the editing task itself, and the hedged, unranked variants with honest-provenance caveats mean nothing gets recommended and nothing carries a clear reason for being suggested.

The real recommendation is a "contested span" bench: the ledger's unique asset is the writer's successive settled wordings of one sentence, and diffing those against each other (rather than against the current draft) reveals the stable core versus the actually-contested part — that's the core diagnostic logic. I'm working through the trigger design: the margin tick should name the contested span directly ("Four wordings; the ending keeps changing"), with a manual "Rework" option from selection that behaves differently depending on whether the ledger has history — falling back to a simpler form with just the sentence's job question and whole-sentence model candidates when there's no prior settled wording to diff against.

Inputs needed: the ledger's wordings with timestamps, neighbouring sentences, dossier goal/audience, and optionally Jev or a prose model. The output should render as a single block without tabs — the sentence shown with the contested span marked and the stable text left plain, plus a line of diagnosis stating the tier-0 insight plainly.

Keep as is stops the nagging until the text changes, Cut previews the paragraph minus the sentence, and Hear plays the neighboring lines against the candidate. Accepting applies the edit with undo support, places the caret, closes the bench, clears the margin tick, and marks the ledger entry resolved for later revision tracking. I'm also sketching a before/after example: Morgan's opening line, rewritten nine times, with a margin card flagging the repeated reworking and a tab listing her earlier attempts alongside notes like "No safe rule change" or "Reduce emphasis."

She's shown model wordings labeled as unchecked for meaning, cycles through six near-identical sentences without picking one, closes the panel, and it resurfaces after a cooldown. Afterward the margin tick notes that her opening clause has stayed stable while the ending keeps shifting, and opening it reveals her sentence with the ending underlined, her four candidate endings, a note that two of them reference "the letter" that the next sentence depends on — she can hover and listen to an ending, pick it, or decide the real issue is the next sentence and quiet the prompt with "Keep as is." I'm also noting the Remove flow, starting with a Words tab for single-word alternatives.

Now I'm thinking through what to strip from the design: the Place tab's move trigger, the Compare panel, treating the manuscript itself as the editor rather than a separate textarea, the regex rewrite rules given their low hit rate, the provenance disclosure folded into a single chip, and the context toggles replaced by always showing one neighboring line each side. What stays is the ledger, Harper gate, ghost preview, Hear, a single Ask an editor link, and undo — and I'm sketching the first implementable phase scoped to just the code-only tier.

For that phase, I'm detailing the work: computing contested spans across settled wordings by finding common prefix/suffix tokens with an LCS fallback for mid-sentence churn, feeding that span into the reason text, swapping the Rewrite tab's list for these contested fragments while keeping the ghost preview by splicing the fragment back into the sentence, treating "Keep as is" as a settle action that stamps a resolvedAt timestamp the ledger can later ignore, and stripping the Words/Place/Compare UI from this bench while leaving the underlying code for the selection-word path. Phase 2 would handle the Jev job choice and related per-item logic.

Now I'm thinking through evaluation: an offline corpus of authored ledgers with known stable/contested spans to measure span accuracy, behavior metrics around resolved vs dismissed opens and re-trigger rate after a decision, timing from open to decision including opens with no action, and how room labels factor into the Jev job evaluation.

I should also flag the risks: contested spans get noisy when a sentence is fully rewritten with no stable core, so I'd fall back to showing "all four differ throughout" honestly rather than forcing a false signal. Ledger quality issues (settle timing, spelling) can still produce junk wordings, the near-duplicate collapse threshold might be too tight, and job labels need hedged phrasing like "seems to be" with an opt-out, since being presumptuous is a real risk. I also need to account for the fact that removing Words/Place would break documented, shipped functionality referenced in the manual and demo film assets, so docs and e2e tests would need updates too.

I'm questioning whether the ledger history is actually rich enough in real use — fast single-sentence rewriting may only yield 1-2 settled wordings instead of 4, meaning the trigger rarely fires and the bench mostly gets reached through Rework with no history, which is my weakest design point; possible mitigation is lowering the settled-wording threshold to 2, or treating selection as "name the job" only. I'm also second-guessing whether the user's hesitation is really about the bench's content at all, rather than something more fundamental about how they write.

I couldn't access the JSTOR full text, so I'll flag that the diagnosis framing relies on the paper's widely cited distinction rather than my own verification of the complete argument. I should also note that manual-films.ts and related documentation narrate the current bench, meaning any change carries a documentation cost. Aiming for roughly 1400-1800 words with at most three headers, I'm ready to start writing.

content.text:
**Summary.** The Sentence bench is a well-built wording picker that skips the step a stuck writer actually needs: a diagnosis of what the sentence is failing to do. My recommendation is to turn it into a one-screen instrument that shows the writer which part of the sentence they keep changing, what the sentence seems to be for, and three ways out. No implementation was done and no files were touched.

## What the bench does today (verified in code)

**Triggers.** It opens three ways. The struggle tracker opens it when one sentence has three or more settled wordings in the ledger, scored at or above the struggle threshold and passed through a Jev classification gate, in `src/components/editor/extensions/struggle-tracker.ts`. It also opens on the Place tab after a sentence has been moved three times. The selection toolbar opens it on demand, labelled "Rework" for a passage and "Alternatives" for a single word.

**Content.** The Rewrite tab lists the writer's own earlier settled wordings, rule rewrites from eleven wordy-phrase regexes plus intensifier removal, semicolon split and clause fronting, and up to three model wordings when a prose provider is configured. The prompt asks for reorder, cut, make concrete, with no explanation, so every model candidate is labelled only "Model wording". All candidates pass a Harper gate, and Jev can attach a meaning probability that is shown only inside the "How these were checked" disclosure. Words offers a bundled thesaurus of 38 headwords plus an optional fill-mask pack. Place offers neighbouring slots by rule. Hear reads neighbour, candidate, neighbour. There is also a working textarea with a diff, a Compare panel, Context and Whole paragraph toggles, and an Ask an editor room.

**Return path.** Use this wording re-lints, checks the sentence is unchanged, inserts with a closed history step, closes the bench and cools the paragraph down for five minutes. Hover previews the candidate as ghost text in place. This part is good and should survive.

**How often the local tier has anything to say.** I ran the rule and thesaurus functions on eight sentences I wrote, three of them deliberately containing trigger phrases. This is an illustration, not a measurement.

| Sentence type | Rule rewrites | Words with thesaurus entries |
|---|---|---|
| 5 ordinary literary or essay sentences | 0 on four, 1 on one | 0 to 2 each |
| 3 planted with "in order to", "made a decision", "very" | 1 to 2 each | 1 to 3 each |

So on prose a careful writer actually produces, the offline Rewrite tab usually shows "No safe rule change", and the Words tab has entries for one word in a sentence if any.

## Why a writer does not reach for it

**It detects and proposes but never diagnoses.** Flower, Hayes, Carey, Schriver and Stratman separate detecting that something is wrong, diagnosing what is wrong, and choosing a strategy, in "Detection, Diagnosis, and the Strategies of Revision", College Composition and Communication 37(1), 1986 ([doi:10.2307/357381](https://doi.org/10.2307/357381)). I verified the citation but could not load the full text in this session, so I am leaning on the paper's widely cited distinction rather than quoting it. The bench does detection well ("You've reworded one sentence 4 times") and jumps straight to candidates. A writer on their fourth version has already rejected three wordings. Showing those back, plus surface transforms and three unlabelled model sentences, gives them nothing they did not have.

**It is built for the rewording model of revision.** Sommers found that student writers treat revision as rewording while experienced writers revise for meaning and the reader, in "Revision Strategies of Student Writers and Experienced Adult Writers", CCC 31(4), 1980 ([ERIC EJ240356](https://eric.ed.gov/?id=EJ240356), [doi:10.2307/356588](https://doi.org/10.2307/356588)). Every pane of the bench operates at the word or wording level. The one thing it could say about meaning, the Jev probability, is hidden in a disclosure.

**It carries a lot of surface for one sentence.** Four tabs, a textarea that duplicates the editor, Compare, two context toggles, an About disclosure and a room. The manuscript already offers in-place editing with undo. The bench's genuine advantages over the editor are the ledger history, ghost preview, and Hear. The rest is weight.

**Every item is hedged and nothing is recommended.** The provenance honesty is right for this product, but a list where every entry says "meaning has not been checked" leaves the writer exactly as undecided as before. Inference, not evidence: I believe this is the root of "I cannot see myself using it". There is no user research behind that claim.

**It fires late and then nags.** The trigger needs three settled wordings, a five second settle each, and the Jev gate. By then the writer is either done or deep in it. Dismissal cools the paragraph for five minutes and the same card returns.

## Recommendation: show the contested span, then ask for one decision

The ledger holds something no other writing tool has: successive settled wordings of one sentence. Diffing those wordings against each other, not against the current text, yields a diagnosis in pure code: the stable core the writer never touched, and the contested span they keep rewriting.

**Trigger.** Same settled-wording signal, but the margin tick's reason names the finding: "Four wordings. The opening clause has stayed; the ending keeps changing." Per the autonomy memory, that line appears with no click. The bench opens on click, or from "Rework" when the ledger has at least two wordings for the selected sentence.

**Input and context.** The ledger entry's wordings with timestamps, one neighbouring sentence on each side, and the dossier goal and audience. Jev when available. A prose provider when configured.

**Visible output, one block, no tabs.**
- The sentence as it stands, stable text plain, contested span marked.
- One diagnosis line. Tier 0: the stable and contested description above. Tier 2, Jev: "This sentence seems to be setting up 'the letter' in the next one", from a Choice over a small authored list of sentence jobs, with its probability, plus a per-wording Noul "does this wording do that job" that orders the writer's own versions. Tier 3, prose model: one sentence naming the tension between the writer's versions, by number ("Versions 1 and 3 lead with the grief; 2 and 4 with the room. Which should the reader meet first?"), and at most two candidates that change only the contested span, each tagged with the choice it makes.
- The writer's contested-span variants as fragments in the order tried, each hover-previewing in place via the existing ghost path, each with Hear.

**Writer decision.** Three actions. Use this one. Keep as is and stop asking, which records a resolution on the ledger entry so the signal stays quiet until the text changes, answering the feedback-memory ask in the October 19 UX brief. Cut the sentence, which previews the paragraph without it before applying. Ask an editor stays as one link.

**Return to manuscript.** Apply as one undo step, caret at the end of the sentence, bench closes, tick clears, decision recorded on the ledger entry so the versions page can later lead with "ending of the opening sentence settled" rather than word counts.

**Before and after, Morgan's opening line.** Before: a margin card reads "Sentence bench. You've reworded one sentence 4 times." Rewrite lists three earlier full sentences, "No safe rule change", and three model wordings labelled "Model wording · −2 words". Morgan reads six near-identical sentences, picks none, closes it, and it returns later. After: the tick reads "Four wordings. The opening clause has stayed; the ending keeps changing." Morgan opens it, sees her ending underlined and her four endings as fragments, and the line "This sentence seems to be setting up 'the letter' in the next one." Two of her endings mention the letter. She hovers the second, hears it between its neighbours, and uses it. Or she realises the next sentence is the real problem, clicks Keep as is, and the bench stays quiet.

**Remove.** The Words tab from this bench, since single-word Alternatives already has its own entry point and belongs in a small popover. The Place tab, keeping the three-moves trigger as a separate small Move slip or dropping it for now. The Compare panel. The working textarea. The regex rule rewrites, demoted to in-line hints or dropped. The About disclosure, replaced by one chip per item. The Context toggles, since one neighbour each side is always shown. Keep the ledger, the Harper gate, ghost preview, Hear, undo, and the room link. Note the manual, narration script and demo film in `src/routes/docs/manual-films.ts` describe the current tabs, so this has documentation and e2e screenshot cost.

**Small implementable scope.** Phase 1 is code only: a `contestedSpan(wordings)` function in `src/utils/sentence-bench.ts` using token common prefix and suffix with an LCS fallback, the new reason text in readStruggle, the fragment list replacing the Rewrite list, a resolvedAt field on ledger entries honoured by the trigger, and removal of the tabs from this bench. Phase 2 adds the Jev job Choice and per-wording Noul, reusing the existing batched ask and the meaning-noul pattern already in the tracker. Phase 3 changes the in-flow prompt to ask for the tension line and contested-span candidates only, each with a reason tag.

**Evaluation.** Add authored ledgers with known stable and contested spans to the instruments corpus and check the span function. Track per open: resolved by use, keep, or cut, versus dismissed, and the re-trigger rate on the same sentence after a decision, which should be near zero. For Jev job labels, an authored corpus with acceptable sets in the style of the room-routing eval. The user's own test: does the first line tell them something about their sentence they did not already know.

**Risks and self-challenge.**
- The ledger may be thinner than the design assumes. Settling needs a complete sentence, five seconds or cursor exit, and a Harper spelling pass. A fast rewriter may produce one or two settled wordings, not four, so the trigger rarely fires and most opens arrive via Rework with no history, where this design is weakest. Mitigation: show the tick at two wordings, and before building phases 2 and 3, log for a week how many ledger entries reach two and three wordings. Unresolved.
- When the writer rewrote the whole sentence each time, there is no stable core. The honest output is "all four differ throughout" plus the versions, which is the current bench again. That outcome needs to be acceptable.
- The deeper possibility is that the user does not revise by rewording sentences at all. Sommers suggests experienced writers mostly do not. Then no sentence bench earns its place and the effort belongs at paragraph and claim level. I cannot settle this from the code.
- Jev job labels can be wrong and feel presumptuous. Keep "seems to be" wording, show the probability, and offer "not that" as a one-click correction that feeds the eval corpus.
- The tier 3 tension line is the one piece that could slide back into generic advice. Constrain it to reference the writer's own numbered versions and nothing else.
- Removing Words and Place deletes shipped, documented behaviour. If the parent prefers continuity, they can be parked behind the selection menu rather than deleted.
